extraction_text: Janamejaya asks about the actions of the Pandavas in the forest and the actions of the Kauravas and their allies.
Vaishampayana recounts that after rescuing Duryodhana, the Pandavas left, and Duryodhana returned to Hastinapura.
Bhishma chastises Duryodhana for not listening to his advice against going to the forest, resulting in his capture and rescue by the Pandavas.
Bhishma criticizes Karna for fleeing the battlefield out of fear of the Gandharvas, contrasting his actions with the courage of the Pandavas.

attributes.relationship: Bhishma questions Karna's loyalty and valor compared to the Pandavas

extraction_text: Bhishma advises Duryodhana to seek reconciliation with the Pandavas for the prosperity of the Kuru family.

attributes.relationship: Bhishma urges Duryodhana to make peace with his cousins, the Pandavas

extraction_text: Duryodhana laughs at Bhishma's words, leaves with Shakuni, and is followed by Karna, Dushasana, and others, causing Bhishma to leave in shame.

attributes.relationship: Duryodhana dismisses Bhishma's advice, aligning with Shakuni and Karna instead

extraction_text: After Bhishma leaves, Duryodhana returns with his ministers to discuss strategies for their benefit and next steps.
Karna advises Duryodhana to assert sole rule over the earth and perform a great sacrifice (Rajasuya) to solidify his power.

attributes.relationship: Karna supports Duryodhana's ambition, encouraging a grand sacrifice to rival the Pandavas' Rajasuya

extraction_text: Duryodhana agrees with Karna, revealing his plan inspired by seeing the Pandavas' Rajasuya, and asks Karna to help implement it.

attributes.relationship: Duryodhana and Karna collaborate to counter the Pandavas' success

extraction_text: Karna instructs Duryodhana to gather learned Brahmins and perform the sacrifice according to Vedic rites.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Vedic sacrifice to assert divine-sanctioned rule

extraction_text: Karna suggested to King Duryodhana that he should arrange a grand feast and drinks to display prosperity and majesty.

relationships: Karna is an advisor to Duryodhana

extraction_text: Duryodhana summoned the priests and ordered them to perform the highest royal sacrifice (Rajasuya) for him with generous donations.

relationships: Duryodhana is the king commanding the priests

extraction_text: The chief priest explained that the highest Rajasuya cannot be performed while Yudhishthira is alive and while his father Dhritarashtra is still living, as it would be forbidden.

relationships: Yudhishthira is Duryodhana's cousin and rival
Dhritarashtra is Duryodhana's father and the elder king

extraction_text: The priest instead recommended performing the Vishnu sacrifice (Vaishnava Yajna), which is equivalent to the Rajasuya and suitable for virtuous people, involving kings paying tribute and using a golden plow.

supernatural_elements: Vishnu sacrifice is a divine ritual

extraction_text: Duryodhana consulted with Karna, Shakuni, and his brothers about the priests' advice, and they all agreed to proceed with the Vishnu sacrifice.

relationships: Shakuni is Duryodhana's uncle and advisor
Duryodhana's brothers include Dushasana and others

extraction_text: Duryodhana ordered all artisans to make the golden plow, and preparations were completed as instructed.
The artisans, chief ministers, and the wise Vidura reported to Duryodhana that the great sacrifice was ready, the time had come, and the sacred golden plow was completed.

relationships: Vidura is Duryodhana's uncle and wise minister

extraction_text: Duryodhana ordered the great sacrifice to begin, and it commenced with abundant food and decorations, performed by Duryodhana according to scriptures and proper sequence.
Duryodhana was pleased, and Vidura, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, and the renowned Gandhari were also pleased.

relationships: Bhishma is the grandsire of the Kuru dynasty
Drona and Kripa are teachers of the Kuru princes

extraction_text: Duryodhana sent fast messengers on swift horses to invite kings and Brahmins from various regions.
Dushasana instructed one departing messenger to go to the Kamyaka Forest and invite the Pandavas (whom he called sinners) and the Brahmins residing in that great forest.

relationships: Pandavas are Duryodhana's cousins and rivals in exile
conflict: Dushasana refers to the Pandavas as sinners, showing ongoing hostility

extraction_text: A messenger from Duryodhana arrives at the Pandavas' dwelling in the forest, invites them to attend Duryodhana's royal sacrifice.
Yudhishthira politely declines the invitation, citing their vow to remain in exile for thirteen years.
Bhima angrily prophesies that after the exile, Yudhishthira will throw Duryodhana into the fire of war and offer the Kauravas as a sacrificial offering in battle.
The messenger returns and reports the Pandavas' response to Duryodhana.
Kings and Brahmins from various lands arrive in the city of the Kauravas for Duryodhana's sacrifice.
Duryodhana, surrounded by the Kuru clan, orders Vidura to ensure all attendees at the sacrificial ground are well-fed and satisfied.
Vidura respectfully honors people of all castes and distributes food, drink, garlands, and clothes to the attendees.
Duryodhana completes the final rituals of the sacrifice, appeases thousands of kings and Brahmins with gifts of wealth, and sends them away.
After the kings depart, Duryodhana enters Hastinapura surrounded by his brothers, Karna, and Shakuni (Son of Subala).
Upon entering the city, Duryodhana is praised by singers and people, but some critics claim his sacrifice cannot compare to Yudhishthira's.
Duryodhana's friends counter the critics, praising his sacrifice as superior and comparing it to those of legendary kings like Yayati, Nahusha, Mandhata, and Bharata.
Pleased by his friends' words, Duryodhana happily enters his palace and pays respects to his parents (Dhritarashtra and Gandhari).
Duryodhana's brothers, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, and Vidura pay respects to Duryodhana after his Rajasuya sacrifice.

attributes.relationships: Duryodhana is the elder brother and king. Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, and Vidura are elders/mentors.

extraction_text: Karna stands up and congratulates Duryodhana on the successful completion of his Rajasuya sacrifice, but states he will offer full congratulations only after Duryodhana performs the even greater Rajasuya (implying the conquest of the Pandavas).

attributes.relationships: Karna is Duryodhana's close friend and ally.

extraction_text: Duryodhana agrees with Karna, stating that after destroying the 'low-souled' Pandava brothers, he will perform the great Rajasuya.

attributes.relationships: Duryodhana and Karna share the goal of defeating the Pandavas.

extraction_text: Duryodhana embraces Karna, showing his affection and shared ambition for the highest royal consecration.
Duryodhana asks his friends when he can kill all the Pandavas and perform the grand Rajasuya.
Karna vows not to wash his feet until he kills Arjuna in battle.

attributes.relationships: Karna and Arjuna are sworn enemies. Karna's vow is a direct challenge to Arjuna.

extraction_text: The great warriors and archers of the Kaurava side cheer Karna's vow, believing the Pandavas are already conquered.
Duryodhana dismisses the assembly, and everyone returns to their homes.

The Pandava brothers, agitated by the messenger's words and news of Karna's vow, cannot feel happy. Yudhishthira becomes depressed and anxious upon hearing of Karna's vow, his bravery, and his impenetrable armor.

characters: Pandava brothers (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva)
attributes.relationships: The Pandavas are the primary enemies of Duryodhana and Karna. Yudhishthira is deeply concerned.

extraction_text: Yudhishthira, troubled, decides to leave the Kamyaka forest.
Duryodhana, with his brothers and heroes like Bhishma, Drona, and Kripa, rules the earth. With Karna as his champion, he remains happy and friendly.

attributes.relationships: Duryodhana is the ruler supported by his family and key warriors. Karna is his key military champion.

extraction_text: Duryodhana performs various sacrifices, gives generous gifts to Brahmins, and treats his brothers well, believing wealth is for charity and enjoyment.
